title: A letter that begins with no harm
hook: a teacher writes a short letter for people he will never meet, and among its first rules is no harm

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vachanamrut's heart. Ekantik dharma: dharma, self-knowledge, detachment and bhakti together.

A conversation only reaches the people in the courtyard. So what about everyone else? The farmer three villages over who couldn't come. The family that moved away for work. The devotee born long after the teacher is gone. Tradition says Swaminarayan sat down at Vadtal, in Gujarat, and wrote them all a letter: short, in Sanskrit verse, something a person could carry and live by. It's called the Shikshapatri. And among the first rules it gives every follower, before much else, is this: harm no living being. Today, a letter that begins with no harm.
screen: `THE ONES WHO COULDN'T COME.` → `A SHORT LETTER IN VERSE.` → `FIRST: HARM NO LIVING BEING.`

segments.voice: Shiksha means instruction. Patri is a letter. Followers hold it as his own writing, and many Swaminarayan communities honor the day it was written, remembered as Vasant Panchami, the spring festival. Its first big teaching has a name every Hindu knows: ahimsa, non-harm. It's one of the oldest ideals in Hinduism; the Yoga Sutras put it first among the restraints a seeker keeps. What the Shikshapatri does is bring it down into an ordinary day. In paraphrase, it asks followers not to kill any living being, not even small creatures, and not to eat meat or drink alcohol. Harm can come out of a mouth too, so it asks them not to speak abusively, not to lie and not to steal. It speaks of serving one's parents and giving to those in need. Next, who it's for. Householders and sadhus, married women and widows, even rulers. Each life gets guidance that fits it, and none is left outside ahimsa. Last, how it asks to be used: read every day, and for those who can't read, heard read aloud, with respect. This is why Swaminarayan families, like many Hindu families, keep a vegetarian kitchen. It isn't a diet. It's a promise not to harm, kept three times a day at the table. In Gujarat, in London, in New Jersey, followers still open the same short letter and read what that promise asks.
screen: `SHIKSHAPATRI — A LETTER OF INSTRUCTION` · `AHIMSA — NO HARM` · `AT THE TABLE, IN SPEECH, IN THE HANDS` · `GUIDANCE FOR EVERY LIFE` · `READ IT EVERY DAY`

segments.voice: Think of the last meal you ate, and walk it back: the hands that cooked it, the field it grew in, the lives it touched. For a few breaths, simply notice, without judging, where it did no harm and where it may have. Swaminarayan families offer their food to God before they eat. If you pray, offer your next meal that way in your mind; if you don't, let one quiet thank-you stand in for it.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Shikshapatri, his short letter, and its first teaching: ahimsa, no harm, kept in everyday life. Today's word.
Your line: ahimsa, lived at every meal. A short letter asks no harm, and a kitchen keeps the promise. Until tomorrow.
